title: Vessel activity in the Northeast Pacific
text:
ImportantA first look, work in progress



These maps are a first look at the data for the Bren MESM group project New Wave of High Seas Protections. The numbers may still change. Please don’t cite or circulate them yet.
Setup: data, colours and helpers
# Everything here is read from small files committed to ../data by the targets
# pipeline, so this page renders without BigQuery access.

# Pixel size of the site's data (degrees). It matches the project's other
# cost layers, and the file names in ../data.
pixel_size <- 0.05
data_dir <- "../data"
repo_url <- "https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/mesm-gp-ne-pacific-high-seas-mpa"
bq_table <- "emlab-gcp.mesm_gp_ne_pacific_high_seas.ais_effort_by_pixel_v20261016"

all_years <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "ais_effort_by_pixel_0p05deg_all_years.csv.gz"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
fishing_yearly <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "ais_fishing_activity_by_pixel_0p05deg_yearly.csv.gz"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
monthly <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ais_effort_by_pixel_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
vessel_classes <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ais_vessel_class_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
download_sizes <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ais_effort_by_pixel_download_sizes.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
land <- sf::st_read(file.path(data_dir, "land_ne_50m.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
study_area <- sf::st_read(file.path(data_dir, "small_gfw_bbox_mesm", "gfwbbox_sm.shp"), quiet = TRUE)

# The extent of the data: the study area box pushed out to whole degrees
map_limits <- list(lon = c(-160, -120), lat = c(39, 62))

# Activity groups: fishing activity, and non-fishing activity split into the
# two big users of the area and everything else (tugs, patrol and research
# vessels, fishing vessels when they aren't fishing, ...)
group_levels <- c("Fishing activity", "Cargo and tankers", "Passenger", "Other non-fishing")
activity_group <- function(vessel_class, fishing_activity) {
  group <- dplyr::case_when(
    fishing_activity ~ group_levels[1],
    grepl("cargo|tanker|reefer|bunker", vessel_class) ~ group_levels[2],
    vessel_class == "passenger" ~ group_levels[3],
    TRUE ~ group_levels[4]
  )
  factor(group, levels = group_levels)
}

# Colours: text and chart chrome, and viridis for everything that carries data
ink <- list(
  primary = "#0b0b0b",
  secondary = "#52514e",
  muted = "#898781",
  grid = "#e1e0d9",
  surface = "#fcfcfb"
)
land_fill <- "#e1e0d9"
data_colour <- viridisLite::viridis(1, begin = 0.4, end = 0.4)

theme_site <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = ink$surface, colour = NA),
      panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = ink$surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = ink$grid, linewidth = 0.25),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$secondary),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$muted),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$primary, face = "bold"),
      strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$primary, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

theme_map <- function() {
  theme_site() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank()
    )
}

# Short-scale labels: 300M, 1.2B
short_number <- scales::label_number(
  accuracy = 0.1,
  scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale(),
  drop0trailing = TRUE
)

# kW-hours per pixel on a log scale. Vessel activity spans about nine orders
# of magnitude, from a few minutes in empty ocean to years of engine time in
# port, so the colours run from the 5th to the 99th percentile of pixels
# (rounded out to powers of ten) and anything beyond takes the end colour; the
# legend marks the two ends with <= and >=.
colour_limits <- function(values) {
  10^c(
    floor(log10(stats::quantile(values, 0.05))),
    ceiling(log10(stats::quantile(values, 0.99)))
  )
}

log_labels <- function(breaks) {
  labels <- vapply(
    breaks,
    function(b) {
      if (b >= 1000) {
        scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())(b)
      } else {
        format(b, scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE)
      }
    },
    character(1)
  )
  labels[1] <- paste("≤", labels[1])
  labels[length(labels)] <- paste("≥", labels[length(labels)])
  labels
}

fill_kw_hours <- function(name, limits) {
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "viridis",
    trans = "log10",
    limits = limits,
    breaks = 10^seq(log10(limits[1]), log10(limits[2])),
    labels = log_labels,
    oob = scales::squish,
    name = name,
    guide = ggplot2::guide_colourbar(
      title.position = "top",
      barwidth = ggplot2::unit(16, "lines"),
      barheight = ggplot2::unit(0.5, "lines")
    )
  )
}

# Map one value per pixel (`kw_hours`)
map_pixels <- function(pixels, fill_name) {
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_tile(
      data = pixels,
      ggplot2::aes(x = lon_center, y = lat_center, fill = kw_hours),
      width = pixel_size,
      height = pixel_size
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_sf(data = land, fill = land_fill, colour = NA) +
    ggplot2::geom_sf(data = study_area, fill = NA, colour = ink$secondary, linewidth = 0.3) +
    fill_kw_hours(fill_name, limits = colour_limits(pixels$kw_hours)) +
    ggplot2::coord_sf(xlim = map_limits$lon, ylim = map_limits$lat, expand = FALSE) +
    theme_map()
}

# "drifting_longlines" -> "Drifting longlines", with the catch-all classes
# spelled out
pretty_class <- function(x) {
  catch_alls <- c(
    fishing = "Fishing (gear unknown)",
    non_fishing = "Non-fishing (type unknown)",
    other_not_fishing = "Other non-fishing",
    dredge_non_fishing = "Dredge (non-fishing)"
  )
  pretty <- gsub("_", " ", x)
  pretty <- paste0(toupper(substr(pretty, 1, 1)), substr(pretty, 2, nchar(pretty)))
  dplyr::if_else(x %in% names(catch_alls), unname(catch_alls[x]), pretty)
}

millions <- function(x) scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 1e-6, suffix = " million")(x)
billions <- function(x) scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, scale = 1e-9, suffix = " billion")(x)
percent <- function(x, accuracy = 1) scales::label_percent(accuracy = accuracy)(x)

total_hours <- sum(all_years$hours)
total_kw_hours <- sum(all_years$kw_hours)
fishing_kw_hours <- sum(all_years$kw_hours[all_years$fishing_activity])
first_month <- format(min(monthly$month), "%B %Y")
last_month <- format(max(monthly$month), "%B %Y")
The data here are Global Fishing Watch (GFW) AIS records for every vessel GFW could identify reliably, from January 2015 to August 2026. AIS is the tracking system ships use to broadcast their position, and GFW turns those positions into hours of activity, with a model estimate of when fishing vessels are actually fishing. Over the whole period there are 278.5 million hours of vessel activity in the area.
Everything on this page is in kilowatt-hours: hours weighted by each vessel’s engine power, the standard GFW measure of effort. That’s 967 billion kW-hours in all. Only 0.15% of them are fishing activity: cargo ships and tankers run engines many times bigger than most fishing vessels, so non-fishing activity is about 690 times fishing activity in kW-hours. That’s why fishing and non-fishing get their own maps and panels below, each on its own scale.
The maps use 0.05° pixels and the whole period. The outline is the study area box. Colours are on a log scale and capped at both ends (≤ and ≥ on the legend), so both the open ocean and the busiest areas stay readable. If you want to work with the data, skip to Working with the data.

text:
Over time


Code
monthly_groups <- monthly |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = activity_group(vessel_class, fishing_activity)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month, group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(kw_hours = sum(kw_hours), .groups = "drop")

ggplot2::ggplot(monthly_groups, ggplot2::aes(x = month, y = kw_hours)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = data_colour, linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(group), scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 year",
    date_labels = "%Y",
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = short_number, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "kW-hours per month") +
  theme_site()





Kilowatt-hours per month. Each panel has its own scale.




Two things drive these lines: real changes in activity, and changes in how well AIS is picked up. Satellite AIS reception has improved a lot since 2015, so some of any rise is better coverage rather than more vessels.


Code
yearly_fishing <- fishing_yearly |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarise(kw_hours = sum(kw_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_label = dplyr::if_else(year == max(year), paste0(year, "\n(Jan to Aug)"), as.character(year))
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(yearly_fishing, ggplot2::aes(x = year_label, y = kw_hours)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = data_colour, width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    labels = short_number,
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Fishing kW-hours per year") +
  theme_site() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank())





Kilowatt-hours of fishing activity per year. 2026 covers January to August only.

text:
Files you can start with
These are in the repo’s data/ folder, so you can read them straight into R with no BigQuery access. The data README has every column of every file. readr::read_csv() reads the .csv.gz files as they are.


Code
starter_files <- tibble::tribble(
  ~file, ~contents, ~data,
  "ais_effort_by_pixel_0p05deg_all_years.csv.gz",
  "All activity at 0.05°, summed over the whole period, by vessel class, fishing vessel and fishing activity. The one to start with.",
  all_years,
  "ais_fishing_activity_by_pixel_0p05deg_yearly.csv.gz",
  "Fishing activity at 0.05°, by year and vessel class.",
  fishing_yearly,
  "ais_effort_by_pixel_summary.csv",
  "Monthly totals for the whole box, by vessel class, fishing vessel and fishing activity (no pixels).",
  monthly,
  "ais_vessel_class_summary.csv",
  "Number of vessels in each class, and how many the filters dropped.",
  vessel_classes
)

starter_files |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    File = paste0("[`", file, "`](", repo_url, "/blob/main/data/", file, ")"),
    Rows = scales::label_comma()(vapply(data, nrow, integer(1))),
    Size = scales::label_bytes(units = "auto_si", accuracy = 0.1)(file.size(file.path(data_dir, file)))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(File, `What's in it` = contents, Rows, Size) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"))

fishing_kw_hours <- effort |>
  dplyr::filter(fishing_activity) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lon_center, lat_center) |>
  dplyr::summarise(kw_hours = sum(kw_hours), .groups = "drop")

text:
Bigger datasets
If you need more detail (months, finer pixels, or a single year), it comes from the full table in emLab’s BigQuery project. That needs special permissions, so Gavin pulls these for you: pick the option you want from this table (or describe what you need) and ask him. The table sizes every reasonable option, so you can see what you’d be getting. Every option keeps the vessel class and the two fishing columns.


Code
# How much gzip shrinks these files, measured on the ones in the repo
in_repo <- download_sizes |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(file))
gzip_ratio <- mean(in_repo$csv_mb / (file.size(file.path(data_dir, in_repo$file)) / 1e6))
# Download speed from BigQuery with bigrquery, measured on a 665,000-row cut
rows_per_second <- 40000

format_mb <- function(mb) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    mb >= 1000 ~ paste(scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, drop0trailing = TRUE)(mb / 1000), "GB"),
    mb >= 10 ~ paste(scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)(mb), "MB"),
    TRUE ~ paste(scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, drop0trailing = TRUE)(pmax(mb, 0.1)), "MB")
  )
}
format_duration <- function(seconds) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    seconds < 60 ~ "under a minute",
    seconds < 3600 ~ paste0("~", round(seconds / 60), " min"),
    TRUE ~ paste0("~", scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.5, drop0trailing = TRUE)(seconds / 3600), " h")
  )
}
time_labels <- c(month = "Monthly", year = "Yearly", all = "Whole period")

download_sizes |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Activity = dplyr::if_else(fishing_activity_only, "Fishing only", "All"),
    Pixels = paste0(format(pixel_size, nsmall = 2), "°"),
    `Time step` = unname(time_labels[time]),
    Years = dplyr::if_else(is.na(year), "2015 to 2026", as.character(year)),
    Rows = short_number(n_rows),
    CSV = format_mb(csv_mb),
    `Gzipped (approx.)` = format_mb(csv_mb / gzip_ratio),
    `Download (approx.)` = format_duration(n_rows / rows_per_second),
    Where = dplyr::if_else(
      is.na(file),
      "BigQuery",
      paste0("[In the repo](", repo_url, "/blob/main/data/", file, ")")
    )
  ) |>
  # All activity first, then fishing only; within each, the whole window
  # before single years, coarse time steps before fine, coarse pixels first
  dplyr::arrange(Activity == "Fishing only", !is.na(year), time != "all", time != "year", dplyr::desc(pixel_size)) |>
  dplyr::select(Activity, Pixels, `Time step`, Years, Rows, CSV, `Gzipped (approx.)`, `Download (approx.)`, Where) |>

Some rules of thumb:

The sizes are close to exact. They’re computed in BigQuery from the real data, and one cut downloaded to check came out at the estimated size.
Anything under ~10 million rows downloads in a few minutes and is easy to work with on a laptop. Over ~50 million rows gets slow, and the full table (262 million rows) won’t fit in a laptop’s memory.
Save big downloads gzipped (readr::write_csv("x.csv.gz")) or as Parquet (arrow::write_parquet()), and keep them on the shared drive. GitHub won’t take files over 50 MB.

title: Vessel activity in the Northeast Pacific
text:
What’s in the full table
The full table is emlab-gcp.mesm_gp_ne_pacific_high_seas.ais_effort_by_pixel_v20261016 in BigQuery: one row per month, 0.01° pixel, vessel class, fishing vessel or not, and fishing activity or not. The files above have the same columns, aggregated.







Column
What it is




month
First day of the month (UTC).


lon_center, lat_center
Centre of the pixel. A 0.01° pixel spans ±0.005° around it.


vessel_class
The vessel’s type, e.g. trawlers, cargo, passenger, tug.


fishing_vessel
TRUE if GFW classifies the vessel as a fishing vessel. This is about what the vessel is.


fishing_activity
TRUE for time spent fishing. This is about what the vessel was doing.


hours
Hours of vessel activity.


kw_hours
Hours × the vessel’s engine power (kW).



Only rows with some activity are in the table: a pixel-month with no vessels has no row, so treat missing as zero.

Hours vs kW-hours. Hours is how much time vessels spent there. kW-hours weights each hour by the vessel’s engine power, so an hour from a big trawler counts for more than an hour from a small troller. Engine power comes from GFW’s model (replaced by registry values where they exist), and every vessel has one.
fishing_vessel vs fishing_activity. A trawler steaming to port is a fishing vessel that isn’t fishing: fishing_vessel = TRUE, fishing_activity = FALSE. A cargo ship is never fishing. The pipeline checks every row, so a non-fishing vessel can never have fishing activity. Fishing activity is GFW’s model estimate of when a vessel is fishing, based on how it moves; GFW calls it “apparent fishing”.
Vessel classes come from GFW’s vessel classification model. When it isn’t confident about a fishing vessel’s gear, it falls back to the generic class fishing. Where it has a best guess for one of the gears it predicts well (trawlers, drifting longlines, set gillnets, tuna purse seines, squid jiggers), we use that guess instead. There’s a similar catch-all on the non-fishing side, non_fishing.

title: Vessel activity in the Northeast Pacific
text:
How it was built

The vessel list. GFW’s vessel identity table (one row per vessel, identified by MMSI, the vessel’s AIS ID), using GFW’s “pipeline 5” models for each vessel’s class, whether it’s a fishing vessel, and its engine power.
The positions. Every AIS position in the box from January 2015 to August 2026, on GFW’s “good” track segments only.
Fishing or not. Each position from a fishing vessel gets GFW’s fishing call (squid jiggers use a night-loitering rule, since they fish at night under lights). Positions from non-fishing vessels are never fishing.
The pixels. Positions are binned into 0.01° pixels and summed by month, vessel class and the two fishing flags.

The box is the rectangle in data/small_gfw_bbox_mesm/ (lon −160 to −120, lat 39.89 to 61.55), pushed out to whole degrees (lat 39 to 62) so that coarser pixels (0.05°, 0.1°, 0.25°, 0.5°, 1°) are never cut by its edge. To trim back to the box as drawn, filter on lat_center.
What was left out, and why:

Fishing gear. Lots of AIS transmitters are on nets and buoys, not vessels.
Vessels GFW couldn’t classify, which have too little AIS activity for the model (about 0.2% of hours).
Noisy vessels: MMSIs GFW saw broadcasting impossible positions, or shared by two vessels at once. A vessel that was ever noisy is dropped from every year, so each vessel is in the time series for all of its years or none of them.
Anything after August 2026, where GFW’s vessel identity data currently ends.

title: Vessel activity in the Northeast Pacific
text:
Things to watch out for

The box isn’t all high seas. It takes in a big chunk of the US and Canadian EEZs, the coast and inland waters. Clip to your planning region before you use any of it as a cost.
Decide early what “cost” means. Fishing activity only, fishing kW-hours, or all traffic? They give very different maps, and non-fishing traffic is hundreds of times bigger in kW-hours.
AIS doesn’t see everything. Not every vessel carries AIS, some switch it off, and reception varies by place and over time. Be careful reading trends from raw totals.
Fishing activity is a model estimate, not observed fishing.
Hours and kW-hours add up; vessel counts don’t. Sum hours and kw_hours across pixels, months and classes however you like. There are no vessel counts per pixel, because the same vessel shows up in many pixels and months.
Coastal pixels include time in port, as non-fishing activity.

title: Vessel activity in the Northeast Pacific
text:
Requesting more data
Anything beyond the files in data/ comes from emLab’s BigQuery project (emlab-gcp), which needs special permissions. Students don’t have them, so ask Gavin and he’ll pull the data for you. The most useful request names an option from the bigger datasets table, or says what resolution, time step, years and activity you need.
For reference, and for anyone who does have access, this is what a request looks like as a query. This one is fishing activity by year at 0.1°:


Code
sql <- "
SELECT
  EXTRACT(YEAR FROM month) AS year,
  ROUND(FLOOR(lon_center / 0.1) * 0.1 + 0.05, 3) AS lon_center,
  ROUND(FLOOR(lat_center / 0.1) * 0.1 + 0.05, 3) AS lat_center,
  vessel_class,
  SUM(hours) AS hours,
  SUM(kw_hours) AS kw_hours
FROM `emlab-gcp.mesm_gp_ne_pacific_high_seas.ais_effort_by_pixel_v20261016`
WHERE fishing_activity
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
"

fishing <- bigrquery::bq_project_query("emlab-gcp", sql) |>
  bigrquery::bq_table_download()


The FLOOR(... / 0.1) * 0.1 + 0.05 bit regrids the 0.01° pixels to 0.1°; for 0.05° pixels, swap in 0.05 and 0.025. Because the table stores pixel centres, this is always exact. With access, run bigrquery::bq_auth() once to log in, and to keep queries cheap and fast:

Filter on month when you can: the table is partitioned by month, so WHERE month BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-01' only reads 2025.
Filter on fishing_activity early if that’s all you need: the table is clustered on it, and fishing rows are a percent or two of the table.
Try queries in the BigQuery console first. It shows how much a query will read before you run it. A query over the whole table reads about 13 GB, roughly $0.07.
